transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-11
Time: 09:30 PT / 12:30 ET
Duration: ~75 minutes (recording)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Redwood SRE); Zoe Patel (Peregrine Head of ML), Mark Liu (Platform Eng), Ayesha Khan (Infra), Samir Desai (Data Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Discussed long-context (>128k tokens) strategies: chunking, KV cache design, attention kernel choices, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization effects, on-prem/VPC constraints and next steps to run benchmarks.

[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone thanks for joining — quick intro, i'm ethan from redwood inference. maya and jordan joining to dig into runtime stuff. zoe and team, thanks for sharing the 128k use case doc beforehand, that helped.
[00:28] Zoe: yeah thanks, we want to be able to keep full conversation histories + multi-doc context, so typical sessions are ~50-200k tokens. curious about what you recommend for maintaining quality and latency.
[00:45] Maya: high level, there are two patterns we see: single monolithic attention over 128k (rare) vs chunked/segmented attention with retrieval/overlap. for most prod workloads chunking + smart KV/cache gives best latency/cost combo.
[01:12] Mark: when you say "KV cache" do you mean a single live cache per session or sharded? we worry about memory blowup on dedicated GPUs.
[01:25] Jordan: yeah good q. we typically implement a per-session KV cache with compaction and tiered eviction; older tokens can be compressed or offloaded to CPU/NVMe and reloaded on demand. the runtime also supports a streaming kv window so the attention kernels only touch the active window.
[01:50] Zoe: does that require model surgery? or is this runtime-level sliding window?
[01:58] Maya: runtime — no model re-write for most transformer archs. we use a sliding attention window at runtime and can do either local attention windows or chunked full-attention recomposition depending on quality needs. note: some approximations (sparse attention variants) need model support.
[02:20] Samir: slight noise: earlier you mentioned flash attention — is that a must for 128k?
[02:28] Maya: FlashAttention and related kernel optimizations are very helpful — reduces memory footprint and improves throughput on GPU. but at 128k you also need careful kernel selection: fused MHA, optimized softmax, and in some cases custom CUDA kernels. on top of that, checkpointing kvs to host and rehydrating is often necessary.
[03:05] Zoe: ok, practical question: we have A100s in-house and some H100 in cloud. any recommended batch sizes / mem configs?
[03:14] Jordan: with A100 and 128k context you're memory-bound. we recommend smaller request-level batch sizes (often 1-4) to keep p95 latency reasonable, combined with longer background batching for throughput (async batcher). also consider quantization to 4-bit where applicable to free memory for kv.
[03:39] Mark: does quantization impact long-context accuracy? we've seen hallucinations with aggressive quant on other models.
[03:46] Maya: yes — there's a tradeoff. quantization (GPTQ / AWQ style) usually affects generation fidelity; for long-context retrieval style workloads, we found 4-bit per-tensor quant with outlier handling preserves most perf for many open models. but you should validate on your evals. we'll share quant tuning notes.
[04:18] Zoe: you mentioned chunking strategies earlier — can you walk through a concrete pattern for 128k input?
[04:26] Maya: sure. common pattern: 1) split into overlapping chunks of 8-16k tokens (overlap 256-1024 tokens), 2) run encoder/embeddings per chunk, 3) maintain per-chunk KV and a "global summary KV" that gets updated incrementally. retrieval can surface top-k chunks into the active window. for stricter "full" attention we can do hierarchical attention: chunk-level summaries -> cross-attention over summaries -> final recomposition.
[05:10] Samir: hmm, recomposition latency seems heavy. how do you keep p95 low?
[05:16] Maya: it's about making the critical path small. use fast local attention for immediate response and kick off background full-recomposition for higher fidelity re-ranks. or use a two-pass generation: quick answer from limited window, then refine if needed. also auto-batching helps — separate foreground low-latency lane and background high-throughput lane.
[05:46] Mark: what about the kv indexing: do we store k/v as fp16 or quantized? how much size reduction can we expect?
[05:55] Jordan: storing kv in fp16 is typical; quantizing kv is trickier because you lose alignment in dot products. some systems compress KV to 8-bit with scale params and get ~2x reduction; 4-bit is possible but requires careful dequantization on the fly. again, tradeoff between memory and compute overhead.
[06:25] Zoe: any built-in support for chunk eviction/compaction? or is that customer-managed?
[06:30] Maya: Redwood runtime has configurable eviction policies (LRU, time-based TTL, size thresholds) and compaction passes that merge old KVs into summary vectors. customer can tune thresholds per workload.
[06:45] Zoe: good. on the kernel side — do you use Triton / cutorch or custom kernels?
[06:52] Maya: a combination. we rely on vendor libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN) for many ops but use custom CUDA/Triton kernels for kv cache ops and fused MHA. FlashAttention is included where applicable; for very long seq lengths we sometimes patch kernels for different memory layouts. there can also be platform-specific flags we tune (e.g., enable_fused_mha=true, cross_block_softmax=false).
[07:25] Mark: will enabling those flags break correctness for some models?
[07:30] Maya: rarely, but yes some model variants with per-head scaling or unusual rotary embeddings need special handling. that's why we do model verification during onboarding.
[07:45] Samir: about batching: you mentioned separate lanes for low-latency vs throughput — how is that orchestrated?
[07:52] Jordan: request routing policy. we tag requests by SLO. low-latency ones bypass large batching and are scheduled on dedicated GPUs with reserved slots. background ones go into a larger batcher that accumulates tokens to increase throughput. the runtime has admission control so warm-up bursts don't starve p95.
[08:18] Zoe: how do you measure latency for very long contexts where token generation itself takes long? what p95 do you target?
[08:25] Maya: we separate initial-response latency (time to first token) vs full-stream completion. for long-context interactive apps customers often care about time-to-first-token — we aim to keep that low. p95 depends on model/hardware; we'll run a benchmark with your dataset to produce concrete numbers.
[08:48] Mark: can you explain CPU/NVMe offload — what's the perf hit?
[08:55] Jordan: offloading KV to host or NVMe introduces latency on cold accesses but helps keep GPUs from OOM. we use async prefetching and predictive hot/cold tiering to minimize stalls. worst-case you'll see higher p99s on cold rehydration, but average throughput improves.
[09:15] Zoe: security question — for our regulated data we need KMS/HSM integration and air-gapped on-prem. is that supported?
[09:22] Ethan: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed control plane, KMS/HSM integration for keys, and on-prem air-gapped bundles. Jordan can walk through network/VPC peering and how we handle audit logs.
[09:35] Jordan: we support SSO, fine-grained RBAC, audit trails and can route logs to your SIEM. for air-gapped, the on-prem package runs with local registries and we provide an offline install. note: some kernel-level optimizations (if we deliver as pre-compiled CUDA kernels) need matching driver/CUDA versions.
[09:58] Ayesha: that driver matching is a concern — our ops team is strict on driver versions. how flexible are you?
[10:05] Jordan: we provide a compatibility matrix and can build kernels for your driver/CUDA stack. there may be some turnaround but we usually handle that during onboarding.
[10:20] Samir: about evals — what should we send you to run realistic benchmarks? tokenization stats? doc lengths?
[10:28] Maya: please send sample long-docs, tokenization histograms, typical concurrency and SLOs. ideal: representative traces (anonymized) and a few golden prompts for quality checks. we'll run throughput, p95 first-token, memory/kv-residency, and quality/regression checks.
[10:50] Zoe: earlier you said hierarchical attention and global summary KV — can you give a quick sketch of how summary is computed?
[10:58] Maya: compute chunk embeddings, reduce via trainable or averaged projector to a compact summary vector per chunk, then maintain a small global KV of summaries. re-attend over summaries for cross-chunk context. it's lossy but very effective for retrieval/QA style tasks.
[11:20] Mark: do you persist summaries to disk between sessions?
[11:25] Maya: yes, summaries and compacted KVs can be persisted in a fast store (rocksdb / s3) depending on access patterns.
[11:32] Ethan: okay shifting to concrete deliverables — we're proposing to run two benches: 1) interactive (low-latency first-token) using 128k corpus, 2) batch re-rank quality pass with full recomposition. we'll share configs.
[11:50] Zoe: timeline?
[11:53] Ethan: we'd aim to run benches next week; maybe share initial results by mid-week. maya?
[11:58] Maya: yes i'll prepare harness and flag sets (including kernel flags, quant configs, eviction thresholds). expect a doc + runbook.
[12:08] Mark: curious: have you seen notable regressions when combining 4-bit quant + flash attention on certain models?
[12:16] Maya: occasional numeric edgecases in outlier-sensitive layers. our approach is to hotpatch outlier layers to 8-bit and keep the rest in 4-bit; also validate via eval prompts.
[12:30] Ayesha: network: for private deployment, can redwood help set up VPC peering and private ECR registries?
[12:36] Jordan: yes we provide IaC templates and can assist with private registries and peering. for on-prem we coordinate image signing and registry mirroring.
[12:50] Zoe: any docs on recommended CUDA / driver combos?
[12:54] Maya: yes we'll share our compatibility matrix and recommended driver/CUDA toolkit combos, plus a list of kernel flags we usually tweak.
[13:05] Ethan: great — let's recap next steps and action items.
[13:10] Zoe: recap please.
[13:12] Ethan: 1) Maya to share harness, kernel flagset, and quantization guide by 2025-03-14. 2) Peregrine to provide two representative long-doc datasets + tokenization hist by 2025-03-13. 3) Jordan to provide VPC/on-prem compatibility and driver matrix by 2025-03-18. 4) Redwood to run two benchmarks and share results in follow-up call week of 2025-03-17.

[13:48] Zoe: thanks team.
[13:50] Ethan: thanks all, we'll send calendar invite for the follow-up.
